items.title: Topic Two Opens: The Five Sensory Pleasures, and How Craving Traps a Being

items.zh: 應說想眾生，依應說安住；不了知應說，而招集生死。
items.en: Beings of name and designation take what should be spoken of [as their object], and dwell resting upon it; not understanding what should be spoken of, they thereby accumulate birth and death.

items.zh: 若了知應說，於說者無慮；由無有此故，他不應譏論。若計等勝劣，彼遂興諍論；於三種無動，等勝劣皆無。斷名色愛慢、無著、煙寂靜、無惱悕、不見此彼天人世。此四頌中，初言應說者，謂一切有為法。所以者何？諸有為法，皆三種言事之所攝故。
今此義中，說妙五欲以為應說。又妙五欲，諸餘沙門、婆羅門等，從施主邊以言求索，故名應說。又諸君主於妙五欲，從僕使等，以言呼召而受用之；由是因緣，亦名應說。又諸受欲者，於妙五欲不能自然善知過患，惟除諸佛及佛弟子，為其宣說彼過患已，乃能了知；由是因緣，亦名應說。
items.en: Here, the sublime five sensory pleasures are what is meant by "what should be spoken of." Other ascetics and brahmins must ask for them from their donors in words — hence they are called "what should be spoken of." Rulers, too, summon their servants with words in order to enjoy them — by this same reason, they too are called "what should be spoken of." And those who indulge in them cannot, on their own, come to know their faults; only the buddhas and their disciples, by actually teaching those faults, enable this understanding — for this reason too, they are called "what should be spoken of."

items.zh: 諸受欲者，於諸欲中不正思惟，而取其相，亦取隨好，即於彼欲便生愛染，受用耽嗜，乃至堅著。
又於諸欲不如實知有眾過患。所謂諸欲無常、虛、偽、空無有實，敗壞之法、猶如幻事誑惑愚夫，甚少愛味，多諸過患。亦不如實了知如是少味多患諸欲出離。所謂於彼欲貪調伏，乃至超越，是其出離。
items.en: Nor do they truly understand desire's many faults — that desires are impermanent, hollow, false, empty of any real substance, subject to decay, deceiving the foolish just as a conjurer's illusion does, offering only the barest sweetness while carrying many faults. Nor do they truly understand how to be free of desires so slight in their sweetness and so heavy with fault.

items.zh: 彼既如是不見過患、不知出離而受諸欲；由是因緣，便於欲界生為根本所有諸行深起樂著。又復造作生為根本所有業已，受欲界生，生已死滅，生已殞歿。
items.en: Not seeing these faults, not knowing how to be free of them, one indulges in desire regardless — and by this cause, one becomes deeply attached to whatever conditioned states take rebirth in the desire realm as their root. Having performed the actions rooted in such rebirth, one takes birth in the desire realm again, and having been born, [the intermediate state at once] ceases; having been born, one [in time] perishes [through ageing, sickness, and death].

items.zh: 如是故言：應說想眾生，依應說安住；不

items.title: Verse Two: Renouncing Without Reward-Seeking, and Why the Wise Face No Valid Criticism

items.en: If one understands what should be spoken of, one has no concern towards those who speak [in criticism]; because this is absent, others should not criticise.

items.zh: 若遇善士，得聞正法，如理作意，則於諸欲如實了知過患出離。所謂諸欲無常、虛、偽，廣說乃至欲貪超越。彼於如來所證正法毘奈耶中得清淨信，便於諸欲深見過患轉復增勝；遂能捨離若少若多財寶、庫藏、眷屬、遊從，以正信心，捨離家法，趣於非家。
items.en: If one encounters a good teacher, hears the true Dharma, and applies proper reflection, one comes to truly understand desire's faults and how to be free of them... gaining pure faith in the Dharma and discipline realised by the Tathāgata, one's insight into desire's faults grows ever deeper and stronger; one thereby becomes able to give up wealth and property great or small, storehouses, kin, and companions, and with a mind of pure faith, abandons household life and enters homelessness.

items.zh: 所謂一切生老病死皆悉永滅。
如是出家，無所願求修行梵行。謂我由此持戒精進修梵行故，當得生天，或異天處。彼無如是邪祈願故，於己不見、不恐不慮他所譏論。謂他不應如是譏論、怨尤、呵責，告言：賢首！汝今何為成就盛年，捨現妙欲，不隨親戚之所願樂，而更悕求待時諸欲，誓修梵行耶？如是故言：若了知應說，於說者無慮；由無有此故，他不應譏論。
items.en: Going forth in this way, one cultivates the holy life with no wish for any reward — not thinking, "because I keep these precepts and diligently practice the holy life, I shall be reborn in heaven, or in some other exalted realm." Being free of any such misguided aspiration, one sees nothing in oneself to fear or worry over regarding others' criticism.

items.zh: 此即成就清淨尸羅及清淨見。何以故？由見顛倒，發起於慢；慢所持故，與餘沙門、婆羅門等共興諍論。由此因緣，說如是見為諍根本。
items.en: This is precisely the accomplishment of pure precepts and pure view. Why is this so? Because a distorted view gives rise to pride; and, held by that pride, one enters into dispute with other ascetics and brahmins. For this reason, such a view is called the very root of dispute.

items.title: Verse Three: Comparison's Trap, and Debating From Compassion Rather Than Pride

items.zh: 若有沙門、或婆羅門，依等勝劣諍根本見，心現高舉；由此因緣，遂與餘沙門、婆羅門等遞相諍論。
items.en: Whoever reckons themselves equal, superior, or inferior thereby falls into dispute; unmoved with respect to all three, neither equal, superior, nor inferior remain.

items.zh: 依止我勝、我等、我劣三種慢類，立己為勝、或等、或劣。若聖弟子，非我、我所、我慢所動，乃至亦非我當非有想非無想所動；了知諸行皆眾緣生，於諸行中惟見法性，尚不以己校量於他為勝等劣，況起見慢而興諍論。
items.en: Resting on the three kinds of pride — I am superior, I am equal, I am inferior — one establishes oneself as superior, equal, or inferior. But a noble disciple is moved by none of these — not by self, not by what is mine, not by pride... understanding that all conditioned things arise from many causes, seeing in them only the nature of things themselves, such a one does not even measure themselves against another as superior, equal, or inferior — how much less would they give rise to views and pride and fall into dispute.

items.zh: 彼聖弟子，雖於他所顯揚自宗，摧伏他論；然於諸法，惟為法性緣於慈悲。謂當云何若有於我所說妙義一句領解，如是如是正修行者，令彼長夜獲得大義利益安樂，亦令如來正法久住。不依見慢及為利養恭敬因緣，而興諍論。
items.en: Though the noble disciples do proclaim their own tradition before others and refute rival positions, this is done resting only on the nature of things, in dependence on compassion — thinking: if only someone might grasp even a single phrase of the sublime meaning I teach, and practice accordingly, they would gain great benefit and ease throughout the long night of ignorance, and the Tathāgata's true Dharma would long endure. They do not enter dispute resting on view and pride, nor for the sake of gain and veneration.

items.zh: 如是不為悕求現法諸妙欲故，誓修梵行。彼由如是修梵行故，遠離邪願及諸邪見，棄捨貪求利養恭敬，於一切種皆得清淨。暉光熾然，

blocks.text: Today's verses answer a deva who has criticised a monk. They are about language ("what should be spoken of"), sense pleasure, and pride. Several short passages, including a verse at 0370c02, are untranslated.

The five sense pleasures are called "what should be spoken of" for three reasons: ascetics must ask donors for them in words; rulers summon servants with words to enjoy them; and only the Buddhas and their disciples, by speaking of their faults, enable indulgers to understand them. Venerable Miào Jìng reads 想 here as "name": the names and words by which these things are established.

How do pleasures trap us? By grasping "the mark and the particulars". Master Cháng Bǎi: seeing a person, one first grasps the overall mark, "a beautiful person", then the particular features. He compares desire to "honey on a knife's edge": a little sweetness, many cuts.

With a good teacher and proper reflection, one sees desire's faults and goes forth. But going forth to win heavenly rebirth is still desire. Venerable Miào Jìng: "If you give up human desires but want to be reborn in heaven to enjoy heavenly bliss, that too is desire."

A distorted view gives rise to pride, and pride leads to dispute: hence views are "the root of dispute". Venerable Miào Jìng: pride looks down on others; conceit puts on airs; self-view is the root of both.

Three kinds of pride: "I am superior", "I am equal", "I am inferior". Venerable Miào Jìng notes that even "I am inferior" carries pride: "though I am not as good as you, I still do not concede." A noble disciple is moved by none of them.

When such a person does debate, it is "resting only on the nature of things, in dependence on compassion", never for gain or to defend a view. Master Cháng Bǎi: they debate out of great compassion. This is worth remembering in any discussion of the Dharma: the aim is to help the other person see, not to win.

quiz.q: Why does the treatise say the sublime five sensory pleasures are called "what should be spoken of"?
options: they are written in the sutras
ascetics must ask donors for them in words; rulers summon servants with words to enjoy them; indulgers cannot know their faults unless the buddhas and their disciples teach them
quiz.why: The treatise gives three reasons: other ascetics and brahmins must ask for them from donors in words; rulers summon their servants with words to enjoy them; and indulgers cannot on their own know their faults — only the buddhas and their disciples, by teaching those faults, enable this understanding. The third is the deepest: desire is a topic that has to be taught.

quiz.q: The treatise says desires offer only the barest sweetness while carrying many faults. What simile does Master Cháng Bǎi use?
options: honey on a knife's edge — tasting it, one is cut
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: it is like honey on a knife's edge — tasting the honey, one is cut by the blade; little sweetness, many faults. The treatise itself compares desires to a conjurer's illusion deceiving the foolish.

quiz.q: The verse's first line is rendered "Beings conceive what should be spoken of." How does Venerable Miào Jìng read 想?
options: 想 means name — names and words are established by perception, so beings live amid names and words
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: how should 想 be explained? 想 means name — the name of names and words, which is established by perception. The English treats 想 as the verb "conceive" and does not convey this sense of names and words. He also explains "words and things": various words arise from various things, and things are expressed through words.

quiz.q: The treatise says one cultivates the holy life with no wish for reward. Why is wishing for heavenly rebirth a "misguided aspiration"?
options: Miào Jìng: giving up human pleasures to enjoy heavenly bliss is still desire; Cháng Bǎi: the form and formless heavens lack sensual desire, but attachment to meditation is another kind of desire
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: if you give up human desires but want to be reborn in heaven to enjoy heavenly bliss, that too is desire. Master Cháng Bǎi: wanting heavenly rebirth is also desire; the form and formless heavens have no sensual desire, but attachment to meditation is another kind of desire. Free of such aspiration, one sees nothing in oneself to fear regarding others' criticism.

quiz.q: How does Venerable Miào Jìng distinguish 慢 (pride) from 驕 (conceit)?
options: pride is looking down on others; conceit is feeling oneself remarkable and putting on airs
pride towards superiors, conceit towards inferiors
pride is cut at seeing, conceit need not be cut
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: pride is looking down on others; conceit is feeling that one is remarkable — putting on airs. He adds that self-view is the root of all dispute.

quiz.q: "I am inferior" admits being lesser — why is it still pride, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: though I am not as good as you, I still refuse to yield — it has the flavour of pride
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: sometimes, though I am not as good as you, I still do not concede — so it carries the flavour of pride. All three kinds of pride are rooted in self-view.

quiz.q: The noble disciples do proclaim their tradition and refute rivals. On what does the treatise say they rest in doing so?
options: only on the nature of things, in dependence on compassion — hoping someone grasps a single phrase and gains long benefit, and that the true Dharma endures
quiz.why: "This is done resting only on the nature of things, in dependence on compassion." "They do not enter dispute resting on view and pride, nor for the sake of gain and veneration." Master Cháng Bǎi: it is out of great compassion that they debate with others.
